blocks.text: Cf. Michaelis, Supplemm. vol. 1, p. 3, where the view of Alb. Schultens, who understands boats made of papyrus or of reed, comparing إباء [ibāʾ], is also weighed, and Bochart's is defended. Oedmann, fasc. 3, ch. 12, renders אניות אבה as ships of skins (as if אוב and אבה were the same word), and understands light rafts set on inflated goatskins so that they may run the faster, such as the river Tigris carries to this day.
See Iliad 12. 206. 219. Iliad 13. 822. Iliad 22. 308. Odyssey 20. 243 and 24. 537. Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 40, etc.
Leo Africanus on the Nesir, ch. 57: In flight it rises so high into the air that it cannot be seen.

Leo Africanus, as above, on the Nesir: they live on the highest rocks and the summits of wild mountains. Schultens cites some passages from the Arabic poets in his Commentary on the passage, p. 1134–35.

Chiefly from the fact that the eating of carcasses is ascribed to the נשר in Iob. XXXIX, 29. and Prov. XXX, 17., Oedmann concludes that in those places the χρυσαιετον [chrysaieton] is not meant, since it [II, 759] never touches a carcass. This itself is not so certain as to be placed beyond all doubt. For concerning the golden eagle (dem Steinadler, Goldadler), which is the χρυσαίετος [chrysaietos] of the Greeks, Taube in his Descript. Slavon. vol. 1, p. 25, relates that it eats dead horses and oxen; and Forsskål, a great expert in natural history, who always uses the Linnaean names of animals, has this in Descript. Animal. p. 12: The eagle, Nisr, lives on flesh and carcasses. Yet if anyone wishes some vulturine species of eagle to be meant in those places, he will not find me much opposed, since I think נשר should not be restricted to some particular bird of the eagle kind, but extended to that whole kind. See above, note 1. Leo Africanus on his Nisr: when it sees a dead animal, it suddenly swoops down. This is confirmed by Hoest, Beschreibung von Fes und Marocco p. 298, whose words are these: Ich habe auch einen hellgrauen Vogel gesehen, zweymal so gross, als ein Welscher Hahn, der bey einem Aase stand. Die Mohren sagten, dass er wohl mit einem grossen Lamme davon fliegen könne, und dass er viele Schaafe umbringe. Einige nannten den Vogel Ensir, نسر [nsr], andere Gernuk, غرنوق [ghurnūq]. Also worth reading is what J. D. Michaelis said on this matter in Bibl. Orient. vol. 9, p. 37 ff., in his review of Forsskål's book.
